t: This document is the software engineering specification of **NAJDA** (Network for Aid, Joint Dispatch and Assistance). It records what the platform must do (requirements, user stories, use cases and business rules), how it is built (architecture, data model, class, state and behavioural design), and how it is verified (testing strategy and requirements traceability). Every capability described here is implemented in the current code base; planned work is confined to the section on future work.

It is written for four readers: **developers** who need an accurate map of the system, **reviewers and examiners** who assess the design, **operators** who deploy and configure it, and **future maintainers** who must extend it without breaking the rules that keep an emergency service safe.

NAJDA is a unified emergency-response platform for Egypt. A person in distress files a report with one tap; the platform captures their position, classifies the report with AI-assisted triage, places it in a live queue for dispatchers, and lets a dispatcher offer the work to the nearest suitable response unit. Crews accept, drive, arrive and complete the mission from their phones; ambulance crews additionally pick a receiving hospital and stream the patient’s vital signs to it while they travel. The reporter follows every step live and can talk to the people responding.
The platform is made of five cooperating parts:

a: **Flutter mobile app (Android)** for citizens and field responders: reporting, live tracking, chat, medical profile, identity verification, shifts and missions, hospital handoff, push notifications and an offline outbox.
**Next.js web console** for every role, and the primary workspace of dispatchers, hospital staff, facility managers and administrators.
**Spring Boot API** (Java 21) exposing REST and a STOMP-over-WebSocket channel, enforcing all business rules, and persisting to PostgreSQL through Flyway-managed migrations.
**AI model service** (Python, FastAPI): a separately deployable, versioned model-serving component that the backend calls over an authenticated internal HTTP interface.

**Managed services**: Firebase Authentication and Cloud Messaging, Supabase Storage, OpenRouter (language-model triage), Brevo (transactional e-mail), Didit (identity verification) and OpenStreetMap services (Nominatim, Overpass, OSRM, OpenFreeMap tiles).
Shorten the time from an emergency to a unit being offered the work, by giving dispatchers a prioritised, de-duplicated, live queue.
Make reporting safe and fast under stress: one-tap SOS, automatic location, works through poor connectivity (idempotent submission and an offline outbox).
Give every actor exactly the visibility their role requires and nothing more, including a consent-based, audited path to a patient’s medical profile.
Keep the service trustworthy: identity verification, a graduated caller-trust policy that never blocks a genuine emergency, and an audit trail for sensitive actions.
Coordinate the hand-off to hospitals, with live vitals during transport.
Operate in Arabic and English, in both directions of text flow, on phones and desktops.
Account lifecycle: e-mail and Google registration, e-mail verification by one-time code, phone verification, profile completion, password management, administrator-provisioned staff accounts.
Identity verification (KYC) through Didit, versioned legal consent (Terms and Privacy Policy), and a citizen medical profile with consent controls.
Emergency reporting for three categories (medical, police, fire), evidence attachments, live tracking, chat, history and first-aid guidance.
Dispatch operations: live queue, AI priority and duplicate suggestion, unit assignment, cancellation, false-report handling, caller history.
Field operations: shifts with a unit LEAD and CREW, mission lifecycle, live unit location, hospital selection and patient-vitals streaming.
Administration: facilities (including OpenStreetMap seeding), response units, user accounts and roles, first-responder applications, first-aid guidance, legal documents, Firebase reconciliation.
Facility management: a facility manager runs the units and staff of one facility.
Notifications: in-app inbox with push delivery, bilingual content.
Platform services: system status, app-update check, support form.
Direct integration with national emergency numbers or legacy computer-aided dispatch systems.
Payment, billing or insurance processing.
An iOS build of the mobile app (the code base is cross-platform; only Android is built and distributed today).

t: NAJDA is developed iteratively in small, vertical increments: each feature is taken through database migration, backend rule, API, both clients and tests before the next begins. The database schema is versioned with Flyway and validated by Hibernate at start-up, so a code change that disagrees with the schema fails fast. Continuous integration (GitHub Actions) builds and tests the mobile app and the AI service on every change and produces a signed Android release when a version tag is pushed. Business rules are kept in small, pure, unit-testable classes (for example the caller-trust and KYC policies) so that the rules that matter most are the cheapest to test.

r: **Must** — essential to the workflow. **Should** — important, with a workable alternative. **Could** — convenience.
Every requirement in this document is implemented.

Where a use case is available: **Web** (the Next.js console in a browser) or **Mobile** (the Flutter app). Desk roles (dispatcher, hospital, manager, administrators) work on the web console; citizens and field responders use the mobile app and, where noted, the web.
The two roles an employee can hold on a unit’s shift. The LEAD is the unit’s accountable operator: only the LEAD accepts missions, updates status and records vitals.
FR = functional requirement, NFR = non-functional requirement, US = user story, UC = use case, BR = business rule, TC = test scenario.

UML use-case, class, state, activity and sequence diagrams. «include» marks behaviour that always happens; «extend» marks optional behaviour; actors marked «system» are external systems. Blue-shaded use cases are restricted to administrators.

t: Requirements are grouped by capability. Each row is implemented and traceable to use cases (section 6) and tests (section 9) through the matrix in section 10.

r: A visitor can register as a citizen with an e-mail address. The system e-mails a six-digit verification code that expires after 10 minutes, can be re-sent only after a 60-second cool-down, and allows at most five wrong attempts.

Only after the e-mail is verified, the visitor supplies first and last name, phone number, address (governorate, city, street, optional landmark), gender and a password to create the account. Nothing is created in Firebase or the database before verification succeeds.
Registration is atomic across the identity provider and the database: if the database step fails, the newly created Firebase account is deleted again.
Code requests, code verification and registration are rate-limited per client address, and code requests are also limited per e-mail address.
A visitor can sign in with Google. If no NAJDA profile exists yet, the client collects phone, address and gender, and the account is created as a citizen.
The server alone decides whether a profile is complete (phone, governorate, city, street and gender present); clients use that flag to route the user to profile completion.
A signed-in user can sign in with e-mail and password, recover a forgotten password, and sign out.
A user can edit their own first name, last name, gender and address.
A user can change their e-mail address; the change is verified by Firebase and then synchronised into the NAJDA profile.
A user can verify a phone number with an SMS code or change it. A phone number already verified on another account cannot be claimed.
A user can change their password.

An Admin can provision accounts for staff roles. The server enforces the role–facility rules, creates the Firebase account with a temporary password and returns a one-time password-reset link; only a Super Admin can create another Super Admin.
An Admin can search, filter (role, enabled) and page through all users, and edit a user’s name, gender and address.

An Admin can change a user’s role. A plain Admin cannot modify a Super Admin or grant Super Admin; a Super Admin cannot remove their own Super Admin role. The new role is written to the Firebase custom claim, and a facility link that no longer fits the new role is released.
An Admin can assign or clear a staff member’s facility, subject to the facility-type rules for the role.
An Admin can disable and re-enable an account. The only remaining Super Admin cannot be disabled, and a plain Admin cannot disable a Super Admin.
An Admin can generate a password-reset link for a user, mark a user’s phone as verified (audited), and override a user’s e-mail. A Super Admin can override a phone number without re-verification.
A Super Admin can compare Firebase and the database, import a Firebase account that has no profile, remove an orphaned Firebase account, and repair a database user that has no Firebase account.
A citizen with a verified e-mail and phone and a verified identity can apply to become a First Responder with a motivation and supporting documents; at most one application may be pending.

An Admin can list applications, open their documents through signed links, and approve or reject (with notes). Approval requires at least one document, changes the role to First Responder, updates the Firebase claim and creates the user’s personal response unit.

t: Identity Verification, Legal Consent and Medical Profile

r: A user can start identity verification; the system opens a hosted Didit session and records the user’s verification status (not started, in progress, in review, verified, declined, expired, abandoned).

The verification status is written only by the backend: from the signed Didit webhook, from a reconciliation with the provider when a status is stale, or from an audited Super Admin override. A person can start again after a decline, expiry or abandonment.
Webhooks are authenticated by signature and timestamp, de-duplicated by event id, and confirmed against the provider’s decision before the status changes.
Deployments can require verified identity before a citizen may report an emergency. The requirement can exempt roles and can grandfather accounts created before a cut-off date.
A Super Admin can mark a user verified or reset a user’s verification (which also deletes the provider sessions).
The system stores versioned Terms and Privacy Policy documents in English and Arabic. A Super Admin can publish a new version, optionally requiring re-acceptance.

Registration records acceptance of the latest versions. When a version that requires acceptance is published, every user is notified and must accept before using protected features; the API answers 403 LEGAL_CONSENT_REQUIRED until they do.
Anyone can read the current Terms and Privacy Policy without signing in.
A citizen or first responder can keep a medical profile: date of birth, weight, blood type, allergies, conditions (or an explicit “none”), medication, notes and up to three emergency contacts.
Free-text medical fields and emergency-contact names and phones are encrypted at rest.
Sharing the profile with responders is off by default and is a standing consent that can be withdrawn at any time; withdrawal takes effect immediately, even for open incidents.
A report carries a per-report choice to share the profile. The server never attaches the reporter’s profile when the report is for someone else.

Only people treating the patient can read the profile: a dispatcher, an ambulance or first-responder crew member on an active mission, and staff of the destination hospital; only while the incident is open. Administrators are excluded. Every read is audited and fails if the audit cannot be written.
A signed-in citizen can submit an emergency report with a category (medical, police or fire), a location, and an optional text message, in one action.

The location comes from GPS or, where enabled by configuration, a manually placed pin that must lie within a configured radius (default 300 m) of the device’s own position; the location must be inside Egypt and is recorded with its source.
Submission is idempotent: a client-generated request id guarantees that a retried request returns the original incident without creating a second one or repeating side effects.
A citizen may have only one active incident at a time.
A citizen can state that the emergency is for someone else; such a report never shares the reporter’s medical profile.
A citizen can attach photos, video, audio and text as evidence, uploaded directly to private storage through signed URLs, and can add evidence while the incident is live.
Until a unit is assigned, the citizen can edit the original text message and delete evidence. While the incident is active the citizen can update the number of injured people.
A citizen can cancel their report until a unit has arrived, choosing a reason category. Open missions are stood down and the crews notified.
A citizen can follow the incident live: status, assigned units with positions on a map, and an ETA.
The citizen, dispatch staff and the crew of an active mission can exchange chat messages on the incident; chat content is encrypted at rest.
A citizen can list and open their past incidents.
The app presents bilingual first-aid and safety guidance cards for medical, police and fire situations, editable by administrators.
The mobile app queues a report that cannot be sent (no connection) in a local outbox with its request id, and sends it automatically when connectivity returns.
The report address is resolved asynchronously by reverse geocoding and never delays the submission.
Dispatchers see a live queue of open incidents and a list of active incidents, updated in real time without refreshing.

After submission the system classifies each report’s priority (critical, high, medium, low) with a confidence value using a language model; a failure never affects the incident, and a dispatcher can retry.
The system suggests a possible duplicate (same category, within 2 km and 120 minutes of an open incident). A dispatcher can confirm the duplicate or dismiss the suggestion.
A dispatcher can see which colleagues are viewing an incident, to avoid double handling.
A dispatcher can see live unit positions and statuses, ranked by distance and estimated travel time to the incident, and can offer a mission to an available unit.

A unit can be offered a mission only if it is available, has an active LEAD on shift, and the incident is not closed. Concurrent assignments of one unit are serialised so a unit is never double-booked, and a unit is never sent to a report made by one of its own crew.
More than one unit can be assigned to the same incident.
A dispatcher can cancel a unit’s mission at any non-terminal stage; the unit becomes available. If it was the last active mission, the incident returns to dispatcher review.
A dispatcher can complete an incident by override, which closes its remaining missions.

A dispatcher can mark an incident as a false report (prank or hoax, spam or test, malicious). This closes the incident, stands units down and records the verdict against the caller; an Admin can clear the verdict.
A dispatcher can review a caller’s history: previous reports, cancellations and false-report verdicts, and the resulting trust tier.

A caller’s trust is assessed from recent history with decay (30-day half-life, 120-day window). The harshest automatic effect is a 10-minute wait between reports with the emergency numbers shown; reports are never refused outright.
An Admin sees a review list of callers whose trust tier warrants attention.
A Super Admin can delete an incident.
An employee can start a shift on an available unit of their type and facility as LEAD, or join an already running shift as CREW; a first responder starts a shift on their personal unit.
A unit has at most one active LEAD. Starting a shift makes the unit available; when the LEAD ends the shift the unit goes offline, and a crew member leaving does not.
An employee can be on one shift at a time, and cannot end or leave a shift while the unit is on an active mission.
An Admin can force-end a unit’s shift.
The unit’s crew receive an urgent push notification for each offered mission; the LEAD can accept it, or reject it with a reason.
The LEAD advances an accepted mission to en route and arrived; the citizen and dispatch see each step live. The LEAD can withdraw from an accepted or en-route mission.
The LEAD of a non-ambulance unit completes the mission on scene. Completing the last active mission resolves the incident.
A responder sees a route map to the incident and their teammates’ positions.
The LEAD’s device shares the unit’s live location; the LEAD can reset it to the home facility. Positions are visible to staff only.
A responder can review their mission history.
Once an ambulance mission has arrived on scene, its LEAD can see registered hospitals within 30 km, nearest first, and select one as the destination.
Selecting a hospital notifies that hospital’s staff (urgent push and live update) that a patient is incoming.
The LEAD marks the transfer en route and arrived. Arrival completes the mission, frees the unit and resolves the incident when it is the last active mission.

While transporting, the LEAD can record vital signs (heart rate, SpO₂, blood pressure, respiratory rate, temperature, consciousness level, notes); notes are encrypted at rest. Vitals are accepted only for a registered hospital destination.
Hospital staff see their hospital’s incoming transfers with a map, ETA and the live vitals stream and history.
A destination that is not a registered facility can be recorded as free text, without vitals streaming.
An Admin can create and edit facilities (hospital, ambulance station, fire station, police station) with name, address and coordinates, and list them with paging.
Before changing a facility’s type the Admin sees an impact assessment (units and staff that would no longer fit).

A first start loads a bundled list of Egyptian facilities (about 800). An Admin can additionally import hospitals, fire stations and police stations from OpenStreetMap through the Overpass API (ambulance stations are added manually) and backfill missing addresses through reverse geocoding; imports skip facilities already present.
A facility is “registered” (usable as a destination or station) only while it has a linked active staff member or a non-archived unit; the flag is maintained automatically and reconciled nightly.
An Admin can create, edit and retire response units. A unit with history is archived instead of deleted, after a delete-impact check.
An Admin can reconcile unit statuses that no longer match reality (for example a unit marked busy with no active mission).
An Admin can search all incidents and edit the first-aid guidance content.

A Facility Manager can list, create, edit and retire the units of their own facility, and list, create, disable and enable its staff. The unit type and the permitted staff roles are determined by the facility type, never by the request.
Significant events create an in-app notification for each concerned user and a push notification to their registered devices; the inbox shows an unread count and supports mark-read and mark-all-read.
Notification text is produced in English and Arabic and delivered in the language of the recipient’s device.
Notifications are created only after the triggering transaction commits, so a rolled-back action never produces a notification.
Four notification types are urgent (new incident, mission offered, mission rejected, patient incoming) and use high-priority, short-lived push on a dedicated channel.
Devices register and unregister their push tokens; invalid tokens are pruned automatically. Notifications and tokens are purged on a schedule.
The application is available in English and Arabic with right-to-left layout and light and dark themes; the choice persists.
A public status page and endpoint report the health of the platform and its dependencies.
The mobile app checks the latest published release and offers an update.
The mobile app can be protected by a biometric or device-credential lock.
A visitor can send a message to the support team from the public support page.
Significant administrative and privacy-relevant actions are written to an audit log.
Live changes (incidents, missions, units, chat, vitals, notifications) are pushed to clients over WebSocket so screens update without polling.

Every API call except a short list of public endpoints is authenticated with a verified Firebase ID token; authorisation is enforced on the server by role (URL rules, method annotations) and by ownership checks, never by client-side hiding.
Secrets (database credentials, Firebase service account, API keys, webhook secrets, field-encryption key, OTP pepper) are supplied by environment configuration and never committed.
Verification codes are stored only as keyed hashes (HMAC-SHA-256); the registration token is one-time and stored hashed; comparisons are constant-time.
Sensitive fields (chat, text evidence, medical free text, emergency contacts, vitals notes) are encrypted at rest at the application layer.
Evidence and documents live in a private bucket; clients receive only short-lived signed upload and download URLs, and file types are restricted by an allow-list.
Abuse-prone public endpoints are rate-limited; the caller-trust policy slows repeat abusers without ever blocking a genuine report.
Third-party webhooks are accepted only with a valid signature inside a freshness window and are processed at most once.
A patient’s medical profile is shared only with consent, only with people treating the patient, only while the incident is open, and every access is audited.
Users must accept the current Terms and Privacy Policy; versions are immutable and acceptance is recorded with source and time.
Live unit positions are visible to staff only; a citizen sees only the units assigned to their incident.
The submission path does only database work before responding; AI classification, duplicate detection and geocoding run asynchronously after commit.
Lists that can grow (users, facilities, notifications) are paged and indexed; hot lookups (notifications by user, citizen incidents, active units by facility) have dedicated indexes.
Live updates travel over a single WebSocket per client rather than repeated polling.
Retried submissions are safe (idempotent request id, unique index per citizen); the mobile outbox preserves a report across connectivity loss.
Concurrent actions on the same unit or mission are safe: pessimistic locking on unit assignment, optimistic version checks on incidents and missions.
Failure of an external service (language model, push, geocoder, mail) degrades only its own feature; core reporting and dispatch continue.
Cross-system changes that cannot be one transaction (identity provider and database) use compensation so no half-created state remains.
Reporting takes one deliberate action from the home screen; the interface supports English and Arabic with correct right-to-left layout, and light and dark themes.
The system explains refusals in plain language, including the emergency numbers (122 police, 123 ambulance, 180 fire) whenever a report is slowed.
The schema is changed only through versioned Flyway migrations and validated against the entities at start-up.
Business rules that decide safety-critical outcomes are isolated in pure classes with unit tests (caller trust, KYC policy, webhook verification, OTP, facility and role policies).
The backend is organised by feature module with a consistent controller–service–repository layering.
Health and status endpoints are public; significant events are logged; the audit log records privacy-relevant actions with actor, target and detail.
Every service ships as a container image or a single archive; configuration is entirely environment-driven, so the stack runs locally with one Compose file.
The web console supports current evergreen browsers; the mobile app supports Android, with the code base cross-platform.

t: This chapter specifies the behaviour of the system from the actors’ point of view. Each group opens with a use-case diagram and is followed by a specification of every use case: actor, platform, preconditions, postconditions, main flow and alternate or exceptional flows. Use-case identifiers are stable and used in the traceability matrix (section 10).
These use cases cover how people join the platform, prove who they are, consent to the terms and are administered. Blue-shaded use cases belong to administrators.

u.name: Register with E-mail and Code
u.pre: The visitor has no NAJDA account for the e-mail address.
u.post: A verified Firebase account and a NAJDA citizen profile exist, the latest Terms and Privacy Policy are accepted, and the user can sign in.
u.fail: Nothing exists in Firebase or in the database.
main: The visitor chooses Register and enters an e-mail address.
The system rate-limits the request, checks the address is free, and e-mails a six-digit code valid for 10 minutes (only a keyed hash is stored).
The visitor enters the code.
The system verifies it, and returns a one-time registration token valid for 15 minutes.
The visitor enters first and last name, phone number, address, gender and a password, and accepts the Terms and Privacy Policy.

The system validates the token, the e-mail and the phone number, creates the Firebase account (e-mail already verified), and in one database transaction saves the citizen, records the acceptance and consumes the verification; then it writes the role claim.
The client signs the user in and opens the home screen; the profile is already complete.
alts: Alternate flow — e-mail already registered:
At step 2 the system answers with a conflict and the client offers to sign in instead.
Alternate flow — wrong, expired or exhausted code:

The system counts the failed attempt (kept even though the request fails). After five wrong attempts the visitor must request a new code; a new code can be requested only after the 60-second cool-down.
Exception flow — phone or password rejected:
A phone number already verified on another account, or a password that fails the Firebase password policy, is rejected before or without creating anything, with a message the visitor can act on.
Exception flow — database failure:
The newly created Firebase account is deleted again, so a retry starts clean.

u.name: Sign In with Google
u.pre: The visitor has a Google account.
u.post: The user is signed in; for a first sign-in a citizen profile exists with the latest legal documents accepted.
main: The visitor chooses Continue with Google and authenticates with Google.
The client asks the API for the current profile with the Firebase ID token.
If no profile exists, the client collects phone, address and gender and shows the Terms and Privacy Policy.
The client calls the registration endpoint; the server creates the citizen, records acceptance and sets the role claim.
The client routes the user according to the server’s profile-completeness flag.
alts: Alternate flow — profile exists:
At step 2 the profile is returned and the user goes straight to the home screen.
Alternate flow — sign-in cancelled:
The client stays on the sign-in screen; nothing is created.

u.name: Complete Profile
u.pre: The user is signed in and the server reports the profile as incomplete.
u.post: Phone, address and gender are stored and the profile is flagged complete.
main: The client routes the user to the profile-completion screen.
The user enters phone number, governorate, city, street, optional landmark and gender.
The client submits; the server stores the data and re-evaluates completeness (phone, governorate, city, street and gender present).
The client continues to phone verification (UC-7) or the home screen.
alts: Exception flow — invalid data:
The server rejects missing or malformed fields and the screen shows which.

u.name: Sign In and Recover Password
u.pre: The user has an account.
u.post: The user holds a valid session and sees the workspace for their role.
main: The user enters e-mail and password (or uses Google).
Firebase authenticates and returns an ID token.
The client loads the profile; the server verifies the token, loads the user and applies the role.
The client opens the role’s home: citizens and responders the mobile home, desk roles their console workspace.
alts: Alternate flow — forgotten password:
The user chooses Forgot password and enters their e-mail.
Firebase sends a reset link; the user chooses a new password and signs in.
Exception flow — disabled account:
The server refuses the token with a clear message and the client signs the user out.
Exception flow — wrong credentials:
Firebase rejects the sign-in and the client shows the reason.

u.name: Manage Own Profile
u.pre: The user is signed in.
u.post: The changed profile fields are stored.
main: The user opens Account.
The user edits first name, last name, gender and address.
The server validates, saves and re-evaluates profile completeness.
The screen shows the updated profile.
alts: Exception flow — address removed:
An address is required; the server rejects an empty one.

u.name: Change E-mail
u.pre: The user is signed in and recently authenticated.
u.post: The new address is verified in Firebase and synchronised into the NAJDA profile.
main: The user enters a new e-mail address.
Firebase sends a verification message to it; the user confirms.
The client calls the synchronisation endpoint.
The server reads the verified address from Firebase and updates the profile.
alts: Exception flow — address in use:
Firebase or the database rejects it and nothing changes.

u.name: Verify or Change Phone Number
u.pre: The user is signed in.
u.post: The phone number is marked verified on exactly one account.
main: The user enters a phone number; the server stores it as unverified.
Firebase sends an SMS code; the user enters it.
The client calls the synchronisation endpoint.
The server reads the verified phone from Firebase and marks the profile verified.
alts: Exception flow — number already verified elsewhere:
The server refuses; a number can be verified on one account only.
Alternate flow — administrator assistance:
An Admin can mark the phone verified (audited); a Super Admin can override the number without re-verification (UC-13, UC-19).

u.name: Change Password
u.pre: The user signed in with a password.
u.post: The password is changed in Firebase.
main: The user opens security settings and re-enters the current password.
The user enters a new password that meets the policy.
Firebase updates the credential.
alts: Exception flow — policy not met:
Firebase rejects the password and the client explains the policy.

u.name: Accept Terms and Privacy Policy
u.pre: A version that requires acceptance has been published and the user has not accepted it.
u.post: An acceptance row records the user, the version, the source (web or mobile) and the time.
main: The user calls a protected feature; the server answers 403 LEGAL_CONSENT_REQUIRED.
The client shows the current Terms and Privacy Policy in the user’s language.
The user accepts; the client posts the consent.
The server records the acceptance of the latest versions and the client retries the original action.
alts: Alternate flow — new version published:
Publishing (UC-57) sends every user a LEGAL_UPDATED notification; the next protected call triggers this flow.

u.name: Verify Identity
u.pre: The user is signed in and not yet verified.
u.post: The user’s verification status is VERIFIED (or DECLINED, EXPIRED, ABANDONED with the reason).
main: The user chooses Verify identity.
The server creates a Didit session tied to the user and returns its hosted URL.
The user completes the document and selfie check in Didit.
Didit calls the signed webhook; the server verifies signature and freshness, ignores duplicates, confirms the decision with Didit and updates the status.
The app reads the status when it resumes and shows the outcome.
alts: Alternate flow — webhook delayed:
The status request reconciles an unsettled status directly with the provider (self-healing).
Alternate flow — declined, expired or abandoned:
The user sees the reason and can start a new session.
Alternate flow — in review:
A person at the provider is reviewing; the status moves to VERIFIED or DECLINED later.

u.name: Manage Medical Profile
u.pre: The user is signed in.
u.post: The profile, its consent flag and up to three emergency contacts are stored; free-text fields are encrypted.
main: The user opens Medical profile.
The user enters date of birth, weight, blood type, allergies and conditions (or confirms none), medication, notes and emergency contacts.
The user chooses whether responders may see the profile (off by default).
The server validates and stores it.
alts: Alternate flow — withdraw consent:
The user turns sharing off; from that moment no responder can read the profile, including on open incidents.
Alternate flow — delete profile:
The user deletes the profile and all its parts.

u.name: Provision Employee Account
u.pre: The actor is signed in as Admin or Super Admin.
u.post: The employee has a Firebase account and a NAJDA profile with the role (and facility) set; a one-time password-reset link was returned.
main: The Admin opens user administration and chooses Create employee.
The Admin enters name, e-mail, role and, where the role needs one, the facility.
The server checks the role–facility rules (for example a firefighter needs a fire station; an ambulance crew member an ambulance station or hospital).
The server creates the Firebase account with a temporary password, saves the profile (creating the personal unit for a first responder), sets the role claim and generates a reset link.
The console shows the link once; the Admin hands it to the employee, who sets a password and signs in.
alts: Exception flow — Super Admin role requested by a plain Admin:
The server refuses; only a Super Admin can create a Super Admin.
Exception flow — facility missing or wrong type:
The server refuses and names the expected facility type.
Alternate flow — Facility Manager:
A Facility Manager creates staff for their own facility through UC-54; the facility type decides the roles allowed.

u.name: Administer User Accounts
u.pre: The actor is signed in as Admin or Super Admin.
u.post: The chosen administrative change is applied and, where sensitive, audited.
main: The Admin searches users by name or e-mail and filters by role and enabled state; results are paged.
The Admin opens a user and edits name, gender or address.
The server saves the change; a plain Admin cannot edit a Super Admin.
alts: Alternate flow — password-reset link:
The Admin generates a reset link for the user and passes it on.
Alternate flow — e-mail override:
The Admin sets a verified e-mail for the user.
Alternate flow — phone verification:
The Admin marks the phone verified (audited as ADMIN_PHONE_VERIFICATION_OVERRIDE); a Super Admin may replace the number without re-verification (audited as ADMIN_OVERRIDE_PHONE).

u.name: Enable or Disable an Account
u.pre: The target account exists.
u.post: The account is disabled (cannot use the API) or re-enabled; a facility’s registered flag is refreshed.
main: The Admin selects Disable on a user.
The server checks the guards and sets enabled to false.
The user’s next request is refused; a live update tells other consoles the user list changed.
To restore access the Admin selects Enable.
alts: Exception flow — protected accounts:
A plain Admin cannot disable a Super Admin, and the only remaining Super Admin cannot be disabled.

u.name: Change Role and Facility
u.pre: The target account exists.
u.post: The role and the Firebase claim are updated; an invalid facility link is released; facility registration is refreshed.
main: The Admin selects a new role for the user.
The server applies the guards, saves the role and releases a facility link that no longer fits.
The server writes the new role to the Firebase custom claim.
For a facility role, the Admin assigns a facility of the expected type.
alts: Exception flow — guards:
A plain Admin cannot modify a Super Admin or grant Super Admin; a Super Admin cannot remove their own Super Admin role; a facility role cannot be left without a facility.

u.name: Apply to Become First Responder
u.pre: The user is a citizen with verified e-mail, verified phone and VERIFIED identity, and has no pending application.
u.post: A PENDING application with its documents exists and Admins are notified.
main: The citizen opens Become a responder and writes a motivation.
The citizen attaches supporting documents (PDF or image).
The system validates and stores the documents privately and creates the application.
The citizen sees the application as pending.
alts: Exception flow — requirements not met:
The system explains what is missing: verify e-mail and phone, verify identity, or wait for the pending application.

u.name: Review First Responder Application
u.pre: At least one application is pending.
u.post: The application is APPROVED or REJECTED and the applicant is notified.
main: The Admin opens the applications list and selects a pending one.
The Admin opens each document through a short-lived signed link.
The Admin approves.
The server requires at least one document, changes the role to First Responder, updates the Firebase claim and creates the applicant’s personal unit.
The applicant receives a notification.
alts: Alternate flow — reject:
The Admin rejects with review notes; the applicant is notified and may apply again.

u.name: Reconcile Firebase and Database
u.pre: The actor is a Super Admin.
u.post: Accounts that existed in only one store are repaired or removed.
main: The Super Admin opens the Firebase reconciliation report.
The report lists Firebase accounts without a profile and database users without a Firebase account.
For a Firebase-only account the Super Admin imports it as a profile or deletes the orphan.
For a database-only user the Super Admin repairs the link.
alts: Exception flow — provider unreachable:
The console shows that Firebase could not be reached; nothing changes.

u.name: Override Identity Verification
u.pre: The target user exists.
u.post: The user’s verification status is VERIFIED, or reset to NOT_STARTED with provider sessions deleted; the action is audited.
main: The Super Admin opens the user and chooses Mark verified or Reset verification.
The server applies the status (a reset deletes the provider sessions first).
The user sees the new status on next load.
alts: Exception flow — provider error on reset:
The reset is refused with the provider error so the state is not left half-changed.

u.name: Report an Emergency (SOS)
u.actor: Citizen, First Responder; AI triage; Nominatim
u.pre: The user is signed in, has accepted the current legal documents, has no other active incident, is not cooling down, and (when required) is identity-verified.
u.post: An incident in status NEW exists; dispatchers are notified; AI priority, duplicate check and address resolution have started.
u.fail: No incident is created and the user is told why.
main: The citizen chooses a category (medical, police, fire).

The app captures GPS (or, where enabled, lets the citizen place a pin close to their position), and optionally takes a text message, the number of injured people and whether the report is for someone else.
The app submits with a client-generated request id.
The server replays an existing incident for the same request id, otherwise validates that the location is inside Egypt, that the citizen has no active incident and is not cooling down.
The server decides medical-profile sharing: only for self-reports, only when the citizen allows sharing now and in the profile.
The server saves the incident (NEW) and any text message, and starts AI priority, duplicate detection and reverse geocoding asynchronously.
After commit, dispatchers receive a live update and an urgent notification; the citizen sees the incident screen.
alts: Alternate flow — retried request:
A repeated request with the same id returns the original incident with no new side effects.
Exception flow — legal consent or identity missing:
The server answers 403 LEGAL_CONSENT_REQUIRED or KYC_REQUIRED and the app routes to UC-9 or UC-10.
Exception flow — active incident:
409: the citizen already has an active emergency.
Exception flow — cool-down:
429 with a Retry-After header and a message naming the emergency numbers 122, 123 and 180; the app shows them prominently.
Exception flow — invalid location:
400: the coordinates are outside Egypt, the source is missing, manual pins are switched off, or the pin is farther from the device than the allowed radius.
Alternate flow — no connection:
See UC-28; the report waits in the outbox.

u.name: Attach and Manage Evidence
u.pre: The citizen owns a live incident.
u.post: The media is stored in the private bucket and registered on the incident.
main: The citizen picks a photo, video or audio recording, or types a text message.
The app asks the server for a signed upload URL (the server checks ownership, that the incident is live, and the file type against an allow-list).
The app uploads the file straight to storage.
The app registers the media; the server confirms the object exists and saves it.
Dispatch and crews open the evidence through short-lived signed download links.
alts: Exception flow — closed incident or bad file type:
The server refuses the upload URL.
Alternate flow — delete or edit:
Until a unit is assigned the citizen can delete a media item or edit the original text message; afterwards evidence can still be added but not removed.

u.name: Edit an Active Report
u.pre: The incident is active (not resolved or cancelled).
u.post: The injured count is updated and dispatch sees it live.
main: The citizen opens the incident and changes the number of injured people.
The server checks ownership and that the incident is active, saves the value and broadcasts the update.
alts: Exception flow — closed incident:
409: the incident is closed and can no longer be edited.

u.name: Cancel a Report
u.pre: The citizen owns an active incident and no unit has arrived.
u.post: The incident is CANCELLED with a reason; open missions are stood down and their units freed; the crews and dispatchers are notified.
main: The citizen chooses Cancel and selects a reason: submitted by mistake, situation resolved, got help elsewhere, duplicate report, or other.
For other, the citizen explains in writing (length-limited).
The server cancels every offered, accepted or en-route mission and frees its units.
The server closes the incident and notifies dispatchers.
alts: Exception flow — unit already on scene:
409: cancelling is no longer possible; the response continues.
Note — caller trust:
Cancelling before any unit accepted costs nothing; later cancellations are weak evidence in the caller-trust score (see 8.4).

u.name: Track the Response Live
u.pre: The citizen owns an incident.
u.post: The citizen sees current status and responder positions.
main: The citizen opens the incident.
The app loads the incident and its missions and subscribes to live updates.
The screen shows status, each assigned unit with its position on the map and the ETA.
Each mission step (accepted, en route, arrived) updates the screen without refresh and produces a notification.
alts: Alternate flow — connection lost:
The app reconnects and reloads; nothing is lost because state lives on the server.

u.name: Chat on an Incident
u.actor: Citizen, Dispatcher, Admin, crew of an active mission
u.pre: The user is the citizen, dispatch staff, or a participant of an active mission.
u.post: The message is stored encrypted and delivered live; other members are notified.
main: A member opens the incident chat; the history loads.
The member sends a message.
The server checks membership, stores the message encrypted, publishes it on the incident’s chat channel and notifies the other members.
alts: Exception flow — not a member:
The server refuses. A person who once took part can still read the history but cannot send.

u.name: View Incident History
u.pre: The citizen is signed in.
main: The citizen opens My incidents.
The server returns the citizen’s incidents, newest first.
The citizen opens one to see its outcome, timeline and chat.

u.name: View First-Aid Guidance
main: The user opens Guidance from the home screen or while waiting on an incident.
The app shows categories of cards (medical, police, fire) in the user’s language.
The user opens a card to read the steps.
alts: Alternate flow — offline:
The last downloaded guidance remains readable.

u.name: Queue a Report Offline
u.pre: The device has no usable connection.
u.post: The report and its media are stored on the device with the request id and are delivered automatically later.
main: The citizen submits a report with no connection.
The app stores it in the outbox and tells the citizen it will be sent automatically.

When connectivity returns, the app resumes or a retry timer fires, the outbox sends the report with its original request id; after failed attempts it backs off from 30 seconds up to 5 minutes. A report saved long ago asks the citizen to confirm before it is sent.
The server creates the incident, or replays it if an earlier attempt had in fact arrived; remaining attachments are then uploaded.
alts: Exception flow — server refuses:
A rule refusal (for example a cool-down or a missing consent) is surfaced to the user instead of retried silently.

u.name: Monitor the Live Incident Queue
u.pre: The actor is signed in with a dispatch role.
main: The dispatcher opens the dispatch workspace.
The console loads the open queue (NEW, AI_PROCESSED, DISPATCHER_REVIEW), the active incidents and the unit positions, and subscribes to live updates.
New incidents and changes appear immediately, with an urgent notification for each new incident.
Opening an incident registers the dispatcher’s presence so colleagues see who is handling it.
alts: Alternate flow — colleague present:
The console shows who else is viewing the incident.

u.name: Review AI Priority and Retry
u.pre: An incident is open.
u.post: The incident shows a priority (critical, high, medium, low) with a confidence value.
main: The dispatcher opens the incident and reads the AI priority and confidence next to the category, message and evidence.
The dispatcher uses it to order their work.
alts: Alternate flow — no priority:
If the language model failed or timed out, the incident simply has no priority; the dispatcher can retry and continue regardless.

u.name: Resolve Duplicate Incident
u.pre: The system suggested a possible duplicate (same category, within 2 km and 120 minutes of an open incident).
u.post: The incident is marked a duplicate and closed, or the suggestion is dismissed.
main: The console shows the suggestion with its confidence and the candidate incident.
The dispatcher compares both and confirms the duplicate.
The server closes the duplicate as CANCELLED, linked to the original, and notifies its reporter.
alts: Alternate flow — dismiss:
The dispatcher dismisses the suggestion; the incident stays open.

u.name: Assign a Unit
u.pre: The incident is not closed and at least one unit is available with an active LEAD.
u.post: A mission in status OFFERED exists; the unit is BUSY; the incident is ASSIGNED; the LEAD is alerted.
main: The dispatcher opens the unit panel; the console ranks units by distance and estimated travel time using live positions.
The dispatcher selects a unit and confirms.
The server locks the unit, checks it is available with an active LEAD and that the incident is open, and creates the mission.
The server marks the unit busy and, for the first unit, the incident ASSIGNED.
The unit’s crew receive an urgent push; the citizen sees the assignment.
alts: Alternate flow — more units:
The dispatcher repeats the use case; each unit gets its own mission.
Exception flow — unit no longer available:
409: another dispatcher or event took the unit first (the lock serialises the race).
Exception flow — reporter on the crew:
409: a responder can report an emergency too, and the unit they crew is never sent to their own report; the dispatcher chooses another unit.

u.name: Cancel a Unit Assignment
u.pre: A mission exists in a non-terminal state.
u.post: The mission is CANCELLED, the unit AVAILABLE; if it was the last active mission the incident returns to DISPATCHER_REVIEW.
main: The dispatcher selects the mission and chooses Cancel.
The server cancels it, frees the unit and notifies the crew.
The incident returns to review if no mission remains active.

u.name: Complete an Incident (Override)
u.pre: The incident is not already closed.
u.post: Remaining missions are COMPLETED, their units AVAILABLE, the incident RESOLVED and the citizen notified.
main: The dispatcher chooses Complete incident.
The server completes every non-terminal mission and frees its unit.
The server resolves the incident and notifies the citizen.
alts: Exception flow — already closed:
409: the incident is already resolved or cancelled.

u.name: Mark a False Report
u.pre: The incident exists and is not already marked.
u.post: The verdict is recorded against the incident and its caller; where it is still pointless to continue, units are stood down and the incident closed; an audit entry is written.
main: The dispatcher chooses False report and selects the type: prank or hoax, spam or test, malicious.
The server records type, time and author.
If no unit has arrived and the incident is open, the server stands down open missions, closes the incident and notifies the reporter.
The verdict feeds the caller-trust score.
alts: Alternate flow — unit already on scene or incident closed:
The verdict is recorded but the incident status is not changed.
Alternate flow — clear the mark:
An Admin can clear a mistaken verdict, which is audited.

u.name: Review Caller History
u.pre: The incident has a caller.
main: The dispatcher opens Caller history on an incident.
The console shows the caller’s recent reports, cancellations and false-report verdicts and the current trust tier.
Admins can also open the review list of flagged callers.

u.name: Delete an Incident
u.pre: The incident exists.
u.post: The incident, its missions and chat are deleted; busy units are freed; evidence files are removed from storage after the transaction commits.
main: The Super Admin chooses Delete on an incident and confirms.
The server frees busy units, deletes missions and chat messages and the incident.
After commit the server removes the incident’s storage folder; a storage failure is logged, not shown.

t: Field staff work on **response units**. A shift ties employees to a unit: exactly one **LEAD** (the accountable operator) and any number of **CREW**. A first responder owns one personal unit and is always its LEAD.

u.name: Start, Join, Leave or End a Shift
u.actor: Ambulance Crew, Police, Firefighter, First Responder
u.pre: The employee is not on another shift; the unit belongs to the employee’s facility and matches their role (a first responder uses their personal unit).
u.post: The shift exists; starting as LEAD makes the unit AVAILABLE.
main: The employee opens the shift screen and sees the units of their facility.
To start, the employee chooses a unit with no active LEAD and starts as LEAD; the unit becomes AVAILABLE.
Colleagues join the running shift as CREW.
When done, the LEAD ends the shift and the unit goes OFFLINE; a crew member simply leaves.
alts: Exception flow — unit busy or LEAD present:
The server refuses to start a second LEAD on the same unit.
Exception flow — active mission:
Ending or leaving is refused while the unit is on an active mission.
Exception flow — already on a shift:
An employee can be on one shift at a time.

u.name: Work a Mission
u.pre: The LEAD’s unit has been offered a mission (UC-32).
u.post: The mission is COMPLETED (or REJECTED, CANCELLED) and the unit is AVAILABLE again.
main: The unit’s crew receive an urgent push notification; the LEAD sees the offered mission.
The LEAD accepts the mission.
The LEAD marks En route and the app shows the route map and teammates’ positions.
On arrival the LEAD marks Arrived.
For a non-ambulance unit the LEAD completes the mission; for an ambulance the mission is completed through the hospital handoff (UC-44).
The unit becomes AVAILABLE; if it was the last active mission the incident is RESOLVED and the citizen is notified.
alts: Alternate flow — reject:
The LEAD rejects with a reason; the unit is freed and dispatchers are notified urgently to reassign.
Alternate flow — withdraw:
From accepted or en route the LEAD can withdraw; dispatchers are notified and the incident returns to review if no other mission is active.
Exception flow — not the LEAD:
Only the unit’s LEAD may change the mission’s state.
Exception flow — cancelled while working:
If dispatch or the citizen cancels, the crew is notified and the unit is freed.

u.name: Share Live Unit Location
u.pre: The LEAD is on shift.
u.post: The unit’s position is current for staff and for the citizen it is assigned to.
main: The LEAD’s device sends the unit’s coordinates while on shift.
The server stores them and broadcasts a unit update.
Dispatch sees the position in the unit list and on the map; the citizen sees the assigned unit.
alts: Alternate flow — reset to station:
The LEAD resets the position to the home facility.
Exception flow — not the LEAD:
Only the LEAD updates the position; positions are visible to staff only.

u.name: Review Mission History
u.pre: The responder is signed in.
main: The responder opens My missions.
The server returns the missions the responder took part in.
The responder opens one to see its timeline.

u.name: Force-End a Unit Shift
u.pre: The unit has a running shift.
u.post: The shift is ended and the unit is OFFLINE.
main: The Admin opens the unit and chooses Force-end shift.
The server ends the shift for every employee on that unit.
The unit is free to be started again.

u.name: Choose Destination Hospital
u.pre: The mission is ARRIVED, the unit is an ambulance, and no hospital has been selected.
u.post: A hospital transfer in status SELECTED exists and the hospital’s staff are alerted.
main: The LEAD opens the handoff panel; the server lists registered hospitals within 30 km, nearest first.
The LEAD selects a hospital.
The server records the transfer and notifies the hospital’s staff with an urgent push and a live update.
alts: Alternate flow — unregistered destination:
The LEAD can instead enter the destination as free text (exactly one of hospital or free text is required). No hospital dashboard or vitals stream applies.
Exception flow — already selected:
409: one transfer per mission.

u.name: Hand Off Patient at Hospital
u.pre: A transfer exists in status SELECTED.
u.post: The transfer is ARRIVED, the mission COMPLETED, the unit AVAILABLE and, if it was the last active mission, the incident RESOLVED.
main: The LEAD marks the transfer En route when leaving the scene.
The LEAD records vitals while travelling (UC-45).
On reaching the hospital the LEAD marks Arrived.
The server closes the mission, frees the unit and resolves the incident when appropriate.
alts: Exception flow — wrong state:
Marking arrived before en route is refused with the expected status.

u.name: Record Patient Vitals
u.pre: A transfer to a registered hospital exists.
u.post: A vitals record (encrypted notes) is stored and pushed to the hospital live.
main: The LEAD enters heart rate, SpO₂, blood pressure, respiratory rate, temperature, consciousness level (alert, verbal, pain, unresponsive) and notes.
The server validates the ranges, stores the record and publishes it on the transfer’s vitals channel.
The hospital’s dashboard updates immediately.
alts: Exception flow — destination not registered:
Vitals are refused for a free-text destination.

u.name: Monitor Incoming Transfers and Vitals
u.pre: The user is staff of a hospital.
main: The staff member opens the hospital workspace and sees the hospital’s incoming transfers.
Each transfer shows status, ETA on a map and the latest vitals.
The vitals history and live stream are available per transfer.
alts: Alternate flow — alert while away from the screen:
The urgent PATIENT_INCOMING notification reaches the staff member’s devices.

u.name: View Patient Medical Profile
u.actor: Dispatcher, Ambulance Crew, First Responder, Hospital Staff
u.pre: The incident is open; the viewer is attached to it in a medical capacity; the patient consented now and for this report.
u.post: The profile is shown and the access is audited (MEDICAL_PROFILE_VIEWED).
main: The viewer opens the incident’s medical profile.

The server checks the incident is open and the viewer’s attachment: any dispatcher; crew of an ambulance or first-responder unit on an active mission; staff of a hospital that a crew has selected as the destination for this incident (from selection until the mission closes).
The server checks the report shares the profile and the patient still allows sharing.
The server writes the audit entry and returns the profile.
alts: Alternate flow — no consent:
The response states the profile is not shared; no data is returned.
Exception flow — not attached or closed incident:
403: you cannot view this patient’s medical profile. Administrators are deliberately excluded.
Exception flow — audit failure:
If the audit entry cannot be written, the read fails.

u.name: Manage Facilities
u.pre: The actor is an Admin.
u.post: The facility is created or updated; the facilities list is refreshed live.
main: The Admin opens Facilities (paged list) and chooses Create or Edit.
The Admin enters name, type (hospital, ambulance station, fire station, police station), address and coordinates.
The server validates and saves.
alts: Alternate flow — change type:
Before saving a type change the console shows the impact: units and staff that would no longer fit the new type.

u.name: Seed Facilities from OpenStreetMap
u.pre: The actor is an Admin and chooses a facility type (hospital, fire station or police station).
u.post: Missing facilities of that type exist; existing ones are untouched.
main: The Admin triggers seeding.
The server queries the Overpass API (with mirror fall-back) for named facilities of that type inside Egypt.

The server skips unnamed entries and any facility whose coordinates already exist, builds an address from the tags or by reverse geocoding, inserts the rest as unregistered and reports created, duplicate and unnamed counts.
alts: Exception flow — Nominatim rate limit:
The batch stops early and keeps what was created; running it again continues.
Exception flow — ambulance stations:
Not offered: they are not reliably tagged in OpenStreetMap and are added manually (UC-48).

u.name: Backfill Missing Addresses
u.pre: Some facilities have no address.
u.post: Addresses are filled by reverse geocoding.
main: The Admin triggers the backfill.
The server reverse-geocodes each address-less facility at a polite rate and stores the result.

u.name: Manage Response Units
u.pre: The actor is an Admin.
u.post: The unit is created, edited, or retired.
main: The Admin creates a unit with type, plate number and home facility, or edits one.
To remove one, the Admin opens the delete-impact check (mission history, live missions, people on shift).

The server blocks removal while the unit is on a live mission or someone is on shift with it; a unit with history is archived (kept, offline, hidden from new work); a unit with none is deleted. Either outcome is audited.
alts: Exception flow — duplicate plate number:
Plate numbers are unique; the server refuses a duplicate.

u.name: Reconcile Unit Status
u.post: Units whose status contradicts reality are corrected.
main: The Admin triggers Reconcile statuses.
The server finds units marked BUSY that have no mission still in progress and sets them AVAILABLE.
The server broadcasts a unit update so every console refreshes.

u.name: Manage Facility Units
u.pre: The manager is linked to one facility.

t: NAJDA is a client–server system made of managed services, an object store and an AI component. Two clients — a Flutter mobile app and a Next.js web console — talk to one Spring Boot API over REST and a STOMP WebSocket. The API persists to PostgreSQL and integrates with external providers for identity, storage, language-model triage, e-mail, identity verification, maps and routing.

a: **Identity is delegated; authority is local.** Firebase proves who someone is. NAJDA decides what they may do, from the role stored in its own database; the Firebase custom claim is a convenience, never the source of truth.

**The backend is the security boundary.** Every rule that protects people (who may see a medical profile, who may assign a unit, who may cancel) is enforced in the service layer; client-side hiding is only a courtesy.

**Safety-critical rules are pure and testable.** Caller trust, identity-verification policy, webhook verification, role–facility policy and OTP handling are small classes without database or clock dependencies.
**Side effects happen after commit.** Live updates, notifications and asynchronous work are registered to run only once the transaction has committed, so a rolled-back action is never announced.

**Fail open for emergencies, fail closed for data.** Reporting is never blocked outright by abuse controls, and a failing AI, geocoder or push provider never blocks a report; conversely a failed audit write blocks a medical-profile read.
**Files never pass through the API.** Clients upload and download evidence directly to private storage with short-lived signed URLs; the API only authorises and records.
**Real time first, push second.** Open screens update over WebSocket; push notifications reach people who are away from the app.

t: The backend is a single deployable Spring Boot application organised by feature module. Each module follows the same layering: controller (HTTP, authorisation annotations) → service (rules, transactions) → repository (Spring Data JPA). Cross-cutting concerns — token authentication, exception mapping, scheduling and WebSocket configuration — live beside the modules.

t: After a report is committed, two asynchronous jobs call a language model through OpenRouter with temperature 0. **Priority classification** turns the category, the optional text message and the context into one of CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM or LOW with a confidence value, stored on the incident (status AI_PROCESSED). **Duplicate detection** compares the new report with open incidents of the same category within 2 km and 120 minutes and stores a suggested duplicate with a confidence value. Both jobs are guarded: a timeout, missing key or provider error is logged and the incident is unaffected; a dispatcher can retry a classification. A configuration switch disables AI entirely, and it turns itself off when no key is set.

A separate Python (FastAPI) service hosts versioned scikit-learn/XGBoost pipelines behind an API key, on the internal network only. A model is a folder containing the fitted pipeline, a manifest that is the contract (features, types, units, ranges, labels, metrics, hashes) and golden test cases. A registry file selects the active version and optional shadow versions, so a model can be rolled forward or back by editing one value. At start-up each package is verified (file hash against the manifest, library versions against the training environment); a bad package is reported as degraded on the health endpoint without taking other models down.

r: The manifest: exactly which features the model expects.

Validate the features (unknown names, out-of-range values and unknown categories return 422) and return label, confidence, probabilities, missing features and warnings; an optional version parameter supports shadow testing.

t: The backend contains the matching client (a typed prediction request/response and a vitals-severity service) so a trained model can be connected to the patient-vitals stream; the first clinical model is a planned addition (see 12.2).

**Mobile.** Feature folders (auth, account, incident, map, chat, responder, handoff, kyc, legal, medical, notifications, guidance, settings) sit on Riverpod providers and go_router, with role-aware routing. Core services wrap the HTTP client (with an authentication interceptor), the STOMP connection, push registration, preferences and the offline outbox, and the biometric lock. Build flavours separate development, local and production configuration.

**Web.** The Next.js App Router hosts one route tree per role workspace. Server state is cached and refreshed by TanStack Query; UI state lives in Zustand stores; live updates arrive through STOMP subscriptions that invalidate the relevant queries; text is localised with next-intl (English and Arabic, with right-to-left layout); maps use MapLibre GL with OpenFreeMap tiles and OSRM routes.

t: Class diagrams show the persistent domain model and the principal services. Only members that explain the design are listed.

`IncidentServiceImpl` orchestrates a report’s life and delegates to small collaborators: `IncidentLocationPolicy` (where a report may come from), `CallerTrustService` over the pure `CallerTrustPolicy`, the asynchronous AI and geocoding services, and `MissionService` for cascading cancellations. `MissionServiceImpl` takes a pessimistic lock on the unit row to serialise assignments, and optimistic `@Version` checks protect incidents and missions. Event publishers wrap every broadcast in `AfterCommit.run(...)`.

Business services call `NotificationPublisher` inside their transaction. The publisher resolves recipients (dispatchers, mission crew, the citizen, hospital staff, administrators), builds bilingual text and publishes a `NotificationRequested` event. The dispatcher component listens **after commit**, asynchronously, writes the inbox rows, nudges connected clients over WebSocket and hands push messages to the `PushSender` abstraction, whose FCM implementation prunes tokens that Firebase reports as unregistered.
Six entities have non-trivial life cycles. The diagrams show every transition the code allows.

t: **Queue semantics.** The dispatcher queue shows NEW, AI_PROCESSED and DISPATCHER_REVIEW; the active list shows these plus ASSIGNED. IN_PROGRESS exists in the enumeration and in the active-status sets but no workflow enters it; field progress is carried by mission statuses.

Trust is derived, not stored: every assessment recomputes a score from the caller’s recent false-report verdicts and cancellations. False-report weights are malicious 10, prank or hoax 6, spam or test 3. A cancellation counts only if a unit had already accepted (submitted by mistake or other 2; resolved, got help elsewhere or duplicate 0.5). Each event decays with a 30-day half-life and drops out after 120 days.
Sequence diagrams show the order of interactions; the activity diagrams show the end-to-end workflow and the validation pipeline of a report.

t: Business rules are the constraints that keep the service safe and fair. Each rule is enforced on the server, in the layer named in the last column.

r: A user has exactly one role. E-mail addresses are unique; a phone number can be verified on at most one account.

E-mail registration: six-digit code valid 10 minutes; 60 seconds between codes; five wrong attempts per code; five codes per e-mail per hour; ten code requests, ten registrations and thirty verifications (per 10 minutes) per client address. A verified e-mail stays usable for 15 minutes through a one-time token.
Registration is atomic across Firebase and the database; on database failure the Firebase account is deleted.
A profile is complete when phone, governorate, city, street and gender are present. Only the server computes this.

Roles that must be linked to a facility: hospital staff (hospital), ambulance crew (ambulance station or hospital), police (police station), firefighter (fire station), facility manager (any type). Other roles cannot be linked to a facility.

Only a Super Admin may create, grant or modify a Super Admin; a Super Admin cannot remove their own role; the only remaining Super Admin cannot be disabled; a plain Admin cannot disable a Super Admin.
A disabled account is refused on every request. Re-enabling clears the deletion mark.
Employees get a temporary password they never see; they set their own through a one-time reset link.

A citizen may apply to become a First Responder only with verified e-mail and phone, a VERIFIED identity and no pending application, with a motivation and files. Approval needs at least one document; it changes the role, updates the claim and creates the personal unit (one per responder).

Identity-verification status is written only by the backend (signed webhook confirmed with the provider, provider reconciliation, or an audited Super Admin action). A settled status is not undone by a late “in progress” message.
When required by configuration, a citizen must be VERIFIED to report. Admin roles are exempt by default and accounts created before a configured date are grandfathered.
Legal versions are immutable and numbered per document type. A new version that requires acceptance makes every protected call return 403 LEGAL_CONSENT_REQUIRED until accepted.
A citizen may have only one active incident (NEW, AI_PROCESSED, DISPATCHER_REVIEW, ASSIGNED).
A repeated submission with the same client request id returns the original incident before any other rule is applied and causes no side effects; the database enforces uniqueness per citizen.
The incident location must be inside Egypt. A manual pin is allowed only when switched on and within the configured radius (default 300 m) of the device position, which must also be in Egypt.
Someone else’s emergency never carries the reporter’s medical profile. For self-reports the profile is attached only if the citizen allows it for this report and the standing consent is on.

The citizen may update the injured count while the incident is active. Until a unit is assigned the citizen may also edit the original message and delete evidence; evidence can be added while the incident is live.

Cancelling needs a reason category; “other” needs an explanation (length-limited). It is refused once a unit has arrived. It stands down every offered, accepted or en-route mission and frees the units.

A false-report verdict (prank or hoax, spam or test, malicious) can be set once by dispatch staff and cleared by an Admin. The incident is closed and units stood down only if no unit has arrived and it is still open; otherwise the verdict is recorded and the status left alone. Both actions are audited.
A duplicate suggestion considers open incidents of the same category within 2 km and 120 minutes. Only a dispatcher confirms: the duplicate closes as cancelled, linked to the original.
AI failures never affect an incident. AI is disabled by a switch and automatically when no key is configured.

A unit can be offered a mission only if it is AVAILABLE, not archived, has an active LEAD on shift, and the incident is not closed. Assignment takes a pessimistic lock on the unit so two dispatchers cannot book it together.
An incident can have several missions. The incident becomes ASSIGNED with the first.

A unit whose current crew includes the person who reported the emergency cannot be assigned to it — the reporter is the one who needs help. When a mission is offered, everyone on the unit’s active shift is recorded as a participant.

Only the unit’s LEAD accepts, rejects, advances (en route, arrived), completes or withdraws a mission. Withdrawing is allowed only from accepted or en route. Dispatch can cancel at any non-terminal stage.

Rejected, cancelled and completed missions free the unit. When the last active mission is cancelled or withdrawn while the incident is ASSIGNED, the incident returns to DISPATCHER_REVIEW; when the last active mission completes, the incident is RESOLVED.

A unit has at most one active LEAD; an employee is on one shift at a time; nobody can end or leave a shift while the unit is on an active mission. Starting the LEAD shift sets the unit AVAILABLE; ending it sets it OFFLINE; a crew member leaving changes nothing. Archived units cannot start shifts.
Only the LEAD updates a unit’s position; positions are visible to staff only; the LEAD may reset the position to the home facility.
Chat: the citizen, dispatch staff and participants of an active mission (offered to arrived) may send; anyone who ever participated may read. Chat notifications never include the message text.
Concurrent edits are guarded by optimistic version fields on incidents and missions.

t: The caller-trust policy exists to slow repeated abuse without ever refusing a genuine emergency. It is pure and deterministic.

r: Malicious 10; prank or hoax 6; spam or test 3.
Zero unless a unit had already accepted. Then: submitted by mistake or other 2; situation resolved, got help elsewhere or duplicate 0.5.
Each event halves every 30 days and stops counting after 120 days.
NONE below 3; WATCH from 3 (appears on the admin review list); COOLDOWN from 6; REVIEW from 10.

COOLDOWN and REVIEW require 10 minutes between new reports. A report inside the wait gets HTTP 429 with Retry-After and a message that names 122 (police), 123 (ambulance) and 180 (fire). Nothing else is ever refused automatically; suspension is a manual Admin decision.
Only the LEAD of an ambulance mission that is ARRIVED can select a destination. Exactly one of a registered hospital or a free-text destination is required; one transfer per mission.
The recommended list contains registered hospitals within 30 km of the incident, nearest first.
Selecting a registered hospital notifies its staff. A free-text destination notifies nobody and accepts no vitals.
Transfer states advance SELECTED → EN_ROUTE → ARRIVED in order; arrival completes the mission, frees the unit and resolves the incident if it was the last active mission.

A medical profile is visible to a dispatcher; to the crew of an ambulance or first-responder unit on an active mission; and to staff of the hospital selected as the destination, from selection until the mission closes. Only while the incident is open, only if consent is on, never to administrators; every read is audited and fails if the audit cannot be written.

A facility is “registered” while it has an active linked staff member or a non-archived unit. The flag is refreshed on every link change and reconciled nightly. Only registered hospitals can be destinations.

A facility manager runs exactly one facility; the unit type (hospital or ambulance station → ambulance, fire station → fire truck, police station → police car) and the permitted staff roles come from the facility type, never from the request.

Plate numbers are unique. A unit with no history is deleted; a unit with history is archived (offline, kept for the record). Removal is refused while the unit is on a live mission or someone is on shift with it.
Changing a facility’s type shows an impact assessment first; units and staff that no longer fit are handled by the change.
Facility import skips unnamed entries and facilities already at the same coordinates; ambulance stations are never imported.
Chat content, text evidence, free-text medical fields, emergency-contact names and phones, and vitals notes are encrypted at rest with a configured key.
Evidence and application documents live in a private bucket; access is by signed URL only; incident deletion removes the evidence folder after commit.
Notifications and device tokens older than 90 days are purged nightly; webhook event ids after 7 days; expired verification rows every 15 minutes.
Medical-profile reads, false-report verdicts and their clearing, phone and e-mail overrides, employee creation, unit deletion or archiving and identity overrides are audited.

r: Firebase for identity, local roles for authority
Avoids storing or handling passwords and gives phone/Google sign-in for free, while keeping all authorisation decisions auditable in the NAJDA database.
E-mail verification by one-time code before account creation
Nothing exists in either store until the address is proven, so there are no half-registered accounts to clean up, and the account is created with a verified address.
No password is ever shown, e-mailed or shared; the temporary password exists only because the identity provider requires one.
Idempotent report submission with a client request id
A report may be sent twice by a flaky network; the second must never create a second emergency.
Pessimistic lock on unit assignment, optimistic versions elsewhere
Double-booking a unit is the costliest race in dispatch; contention on other rows is rare, so versions are cheaper.
A notification or live update for an action that rolled back would mislead people in an emergency.
Caller trust slows but never blocks
An emergency line that can refuse a caller can cost a life; abuse is handled by delay, human verdicts and manual suspension.
Medical profile: consent, role attachment, audit, fail-closed
The data is sensitive and valuable only to those treating the patient; every read must be explainable afterwards.
Large media never loads the API, and the bucket stays private.
The inbox is the reliable record; push is a best-effort alert that is allowed to fail.
Models are versioned artifacts with a strict input contract and can be rolled forward or back without redeploying the API; the service stays on the internal network.
The schema is reviewable and reproducible, and drift between code and database fails at start-up.
One cross-platform code base with a mature location, map and push ecosystem.
